h1: Tasting beer in hot weather: serving temperature and glassware
title: Tasting Beer in Hot Weather | Craft Beer School
desc: How heat changes the way beer tastes, the best serving temperatures, the right glass and how to taste fairly when it is hot outside.
teaser: A beer that tastes great at 4 °C can taste thin at 14 °C. Heat changes more than temperature.
standfirst: Hot weather changes the beer, the glass and your tongue. This guide covers serving temperature, glassware and simple habits for tasting well in the heat.
sections:
Cold numbs flavour and aroma. Warm beer releases more aroma and shows more sweetness and bitterness. That is why a very cold lager seems refreshing and clean. The same beer at room temperature can taste sweet, heavy or faulty. Neither is wrong, but it explains why a beer seems different from one place to the next.

Read how to taste beer for the method. This guide adds what changes when the air is hot.

As a rough guide, many pale lagers and light wheat beers are served around 3 to 6 °C (37 to 43 °F). Pale ales and IPAs suit about 6 to 9 °C (43 to 48 °F). Stouts, strong ales and barley wines open up at 10 to 13 °C (50 to 55 °F). These are guidelines, not laws. If a beer tastes flat and dull, let it warm for a few minutes.

In hot weather beer warms quickly in the glass. A beer that starts at 4 °C may be 15 °C in half an hour on a terrace. Pour smaller amounts and keep the bottle in an ice bucket or an insulated sleeve. Finish your glass before it warms.

Use a thermometer once. Most people guess too warm or too cold. A quick reading corrects your sense of what 8 °C actually feels like.

Choose a clean glass. Grease and detergent residue ruin foam. Rinse in cold water before pouring. A tulip or stemmed glass concentrates aroma and keeps your hand away from the bowl, which slows warming. A thin-walled glass warms quickly, so some tasters prefer a thicker one for hot days.

Do not freeze glasses for a tasting. A frosted glass dulls aroma and makes foam collapse. A cool, dry glass is better. Use a glass of the same size for every beer you compare.

Wash glasses by hand with unscented detergent and air dry them upside down on a clean rack.
Your own senses in the heat

Heat dehydrates you. A dry mouth tastes less. Drink water between beers. Eat plain bread or crackers. Avoid strong spices, mint and chewing gum before a session. Stay in the shade if you can. Humidity and strong outdoor smells such as cooking smoke or flowers confuse aroma.

Pace yourself. Small pours are enough for tasting. Spit cups are normal for serious sessions. Never drive after tasting. Respect anyone who prefers not to drink.

Sunscreen and insect repellent smell strong. Wash your hands before you taste, or hold the glass by the stem.
Taste fairly in a hot room

Compare beers at the same temperature. Pour them in the same order each time, from lighter to stronger and from less to more hoppy. Cover the glass with a coaster between sniffs to hold aroma. Note the temperature of the beer and the room on your sheet, since your notes mean more with that context.

If you meet a beer at a festival or a hot market, ask how it has been stored. Beer kept warm for weeks tastes stale. No glass will fix it. See learning about beer online: where to start for next steps.
What to try on a hot day

Light, crisp beers with moderate bitterness are common choices in the heat: pilsners, helles, kölsch, some wheat beers and low-alcohol versions. Sour beers, such as gose and Berliner weisse, are bright and refreshing. See the beer styles guide for more. Try a non-alcoholic beer between stronger ones. Choose food that suits the heat: grilled or lightly spiced dishes work well.

Pairings are suggestions, not rules. Trust your own palate.

A beer with a refreshing, dry finish will taste lighter in the heat than a sweet one. Note that on your sheet.

Pour the same beer at 4 °C, 8 °C and 12 °C and write what changes. Repeat with a different style. This takes an afternoon and teaches more than a book. Note what you smell first and when the sweetness appears.

faqs: What temperature should I serve lager?
Many pale lagers taste best around 3 to 6 °C (37 to 43 °F). Adjust to your taste.
No. Frost dulls aroma and spoils foam. Use a clean, cool, dry glass.
Why does my beer taste worse outside?
Heat, humidity, smells and warming in the glass all change perception. The beer may also have been stored warm.
Not always. Some styles open up when warmer. Very warm beer can taste sweet and heavy.
